issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette: Minh was forty-seven when the rupture happened at the downtown medical center where he was retrofitting a central ventilation system. He had been kneeling inside a narrow utility chase, wrench in hand, when a pressurized line of refrigerant and solvent vapor burst without warning. The cloud swallowed him instantly, thick and acrid, burning his throat and stinging his eyes. He remembered scrambling backward, his lungs seizing as he gagged on fumes that the site supervisor swore were temporary, but the panic that followed was anything but. When he finally crawled out onto the concrete pad, coughing until his ribs ached, the relief should have been immediate. Instead, a quiet dread settled into his bones. The smell of industrial cleaners, the sight of yellow caution tape, and the distant hum of a commercial compressor would later twist his stomach, but the memory that stayed sharp was the feeling of the vapor clinging to his skin long after he wiped himself down. Over the following months, Minh’s body refused to stand down. His shoulders remained permanently knotted, his breathing shallow and rapid the moment he stepped into any enclosed space. When his wife gently assured him that the air in their home was clean, or that a physician had confirmed no long-term lung damage, the words did nothing to quiet the vigilance humming under his skin. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion everyone else accepted but he could not. Even at home, his hands would automatically check the deadbolt, the window latches, and the utility room door until his fingers ached, as though securing the perimeter might keep whatever had happened from seeping back in. He told himself it was just being thorough, but deep down he knew it was the only way to keep the invisible threat from catching him off guard. Because his body remained locked in a state of constant readiness, Minh carved his days around staying off guard. When relaxation tried to creep in, he would feel a surge of dread so sharp it made his breath catch, so he deliberately kept busy, flipping through technical manuals or pacing the living room instead of resting. He stopped going to client homes alone, insisting his wife accompany him to every service call, and he began declining overtime or any job that required navigating tight mechanical rooms. What frightened him most was the loss of control, so he avoided anything that could stress his system, trading potential income for a predictable, tightly regulated routine. He told himself these boundaries were necessary, not because he was weakening, but because his nervous system was still reading the air for poison. His work as an HVAC technician, once a source of pride, became a landscape of quiet compromises. He still took calls, but he relegated himself to rooftop condensers and open mechanical floors where the air moved freely, avoiding the claustrophobic utility closets and sealed server rooms that mirrored the chase where he had nearly choked. When his foreman asked him to troubleshoot a complex multi-zone system in a downtown high-rise, Minh’s chest tightened so violently he had to step outside and lean against the brick wall until his pulse slowed. He told his boss he was taking a slower pace to focus on safety, but the truth was that the stress of diagnosing problems in confined, pressurized environments felt like stepping back into the cloud. The more he restricted his movements and the tasks he allowed himself to touch, the more his days narrowed, each avoided stressor simply becoming the next prerequisite for staying upright. It was his wife who finally pushed him to schedule an intake, noticing that he no longer slept through the night, that he flinched at the sound of his own toolkit being packed, and that his hands trembled while holding his coffee. At fifty-two, Minh was exhausted from the constant arithmetic of survival, from calculating which rooms, which tools, and which conversations were safe enough to endure. He had come to the clinic hoping someone could help him untangle the knot in his chest without taking the job he needed to keep their mortgage current, terrified that if he ever truly relaxed, the vapor would return and catch him before he could run.
